reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest pancreatic neoplasm of childhood, typically presenting in the first decade as a large, often palpable upper abdominal mass.
Histologically defined by acinar differentiation with distinctive squamoid nests (squamoid corpuscles), and it may also show endocrine and ductal elements.
Serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in a substantial proportion and is a useful marker for monitoring response and relapse.
Associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, in which it may be congenital, and with familial adenomatous polyposis through the APC/Wnt-beta-catenin pathway.
Abnormalities of chromosome 11p15 and activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signalling are the principal molecular drivers.
Complete surgical resection is the mainstay of cure, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy can downstage large or initially unresectable tumours.
Symptoms are frequently nonspecific (mass, abdominal pain, weight loss), and obstructive jaundice is less common than in adult pancreatic cancer.
Metastases occur most often to the liver, regional lymph nodes, and lungs.
reference.pathophysiology: Pancreatoblastoma arises from pluripotent pancreatic precursor cells and recapitulates the embryonic pancreas, characteristically showing acinar differentiation together with squamoid nests (corpuscles) and variable endocrine and ductal components. The dominant molecular alteration is activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, with frequent involvement of the APC/beta-catenin axis and nuclear beta-catenin accumulation; abnormalities at the imprinted 11p15.5 locus link the tumour to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, while germline APC loss links it to familial adenomatous polyposis. Alpha-fetoprotein production reflects the tumour's primitive, partly hepatoid differentiation. Tumours are often large and encapsulated at presentation and spread to regional lymph nodes, liver, and lungs.
additionalDifferentials: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Wilms tumour or other retroperitoneal mass
Pancreatic metastasis of another paediatric tumour
additionalInvestigations: Serum alpha-fetoprotein at baseline and serially
Abdominal ultrasound followed by contrast-enhanced CT or MRI for local extent and vascular involvement
CT of the chest for pulmonary metastases
Core or open biopsy for histological confirmation when upfront resection is not planned
Testing for Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis where clinically indicated
Assessment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function
Baseline audiometry and renal function before platinum-based chemotherapy
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice or duodenal obstruction from a pancreatic head mass
Rapid abdominal distension or pain suggesting haemorrhage into the tumour
Rising alpha-fetoprotein after resection, indicating recurrence
Features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome prompting tumour surveillance
reference.prognosis: Completely resected, localised pancreatoblastoma has a good prognosis, whereas unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer outlook despite chemotherapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking pancreatoblastoma for the commoner neuroblastoma or for a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm without adequate histology.
Proceeding to a mutilating upfront resection when neoadjuvant chemotherapy could render a large tumour resectable with less morbidity.
Overlooking an underlying Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis.
Interpreting alpha-fetoprotein without accounting for the high physiological levels of infancy.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
European Cooperative Study Group for Paediatric Rare Tumours (EXPeRT) guidance
management: For localised resectable disease, complete surgical resection is the mainstay of cure and can be curative alone in children

A short course of perioperative chemotherapy may be added around surgery in selected localised cases to reduce risk of incomplete margins or occult micrometastatic disease, decided by a paediatric oncology multidisciplinary team

For large or borderline/initially unresectable tumours, neoadjuvant chemotherapy built around a platinum agent plus an anthracycline-based drug is used to shrink the tumour and allow subsequent complete resection
Response to neoadjuvant therapy can be tracked with serial imaging and, when initially elevated, serum alpha-fetoprotein
About one third of children present with metastatic disease, and resection-based cure remains achievable in a meaningful proportion of these children
Metastatic disease management combines systemic chemotherapy with individualised assessment of whether metastasectomy of isolated liver or lung deposits is feasible after response to chemotherapy

In adults, survival after resection is comparable to conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, so surgical resection remains central; when resection is incomplete or disease is metastatic, adults are often managed pragmatically along pancreatic-adenocarcinoma-type systemic therapy lines

There is no established second-line or salvage regimen for relapsed or refractory disease; alternative cytotoxic combinations used in other paediatric embryonal tumours are sometimes considered without a disease-specific evidence base
Radiotherapy is not part of routine management for this tumour
Serial serum alpha-fetoprotein, when elevated at baseline, is a practical way to follow treatment response and detect relapse
Follow-up should include surveillance imaging of the abdomen and chest and prior metastatic sites, plus assessment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function after resection
Refer promptly to a paediatric oncology (or, in adults, specialist hepatopancreatobiliary oncology) multidisciplinary team before surgical planning given the rarity of this tumour
Consider genetics referral when Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis is suspected
